demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Perpetrator' cues are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one; this wording implies an assaultive interpersonal trauma rather than bereavement-related PTSD.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' fits fear of immediate interpersonal attack or entrapment more than traumatic bereavement. In combination with startle/hypervigilance, it shifts the profile toward assault-type threat rather than loss-related PTSD, with no supporting trauma-specific content elsewhere.

vignette:
Arjun

Arjun's father died without warning on a Tuesday evening in March. He was fifty-three, had complained of chest tightness that morning, and by the time the ambulance arrived at their home in New Jersey, he was already gone. Arjun, then nineteen, was in his dorm room two hours away when his mother called. He remembered the specific quality of her voice-a sound he had never heard before, something between a whisper and a shout-and the way the phone felt heavy in his hand as she told him to come home. The funeral happened ten days later. He watched his father's body lowered into the ground on a grey April afternoon, surrounded by relatives who kept touching his shoulder, his arm, his back, as though physical contact might somehow anchor him to the moment or pull him away from it entirely.

In the months that followed, Arjun had slowly come to believe that the world operated according to rules he no longer understood. His father had been healthy. His father had been there. And then, without negotiation or warning, he simply was not. This fundamental betrayal-the discovery that safety was an illusion, that people could vanish in the space between one breath and another-had reshaped how Arjun moved through his days. He became hyperalert, attuned to the smallest signs of threat. His body had learned to startle at ordinary sounds: a door slamming in his apartment building, the sharp ring of his phone, even the hiss of the coffee maker in the shared kitchen would send a jolt through his chest, his heart suddenly racing as though danger were imminent. At night, he lay awake for hours, his mind cataloguing worst-case scenarios, running through lists of people he loved and imagining, with vivid precision, the ways they might be taken from him.

Sleep became a battleground. He would lie in bed at two in the morning, exhausted but unable to surrender to unconsciousness, because sleep felt like a kind of death, a surrender of control. He had come to believe that if he stayed vigilant enough, stayed awake enough, he could somehow prevent the next catastrophe. Even in daylight, even when he sat in his apartment with the doors locked and the windows closed, he could not find the relaxation that had once come naturally to him. His body remained taut, waiting. His therapist had used the word "hypervigilance," but what Arjun experienced was simpler and more terrifying: the absolute certainty that something else was coming.

The weight of this certainty had begun to reshape his life in concrete ways. He had withdrawn from his writing-the thing that had defined him since childhood. He had been working on a novel about a family across generations, but now the manuscript sat untouched on his laptop, and he could not bring himself to open it. Writing about family felt like inviting disaster, as though imagining loss on the page might somehow make it real in the world. He had stopped making plans beyond the immediate day. When his roommate suggested they sign a lease together for next year, Arjun felt panic rise in his throat. How could he commit to anything when everything could disappear? When people he loved could be erased without reason or mercy?

He had also begun seeking constant reassurance from others. He texted his mother multiple times a day, asking her to confirm she was okay, that she had eaten, that she felt well. He called his sister at odd hours. He asked his roommate repeatedly whether he seemed normal, whether something felt wrong with him, whether he was going to be all right. His friends had begun to pull away, exhausted by the neediness, confused by the intensity of his fear. He had lost his best friend to this-Rohan had stopped responding to his messages after Arjun called him seven times in one evening asking whether he was safe.

What frightened Arjun most now was that he had become someone he no longer recognized. The person he used to be-the one who wrote stories, who made plans, who felt happiness as a baseline rather than a distant memory-seemed to have been buried in that cemetery alongside his father. He was twenty years old and felt ancient, worn down by the knowledge that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that everyone he loved was always, always at risk. When his mother finally insisted he see someone, Arjun agreed not out of hope but out of desperation. He was not sure he could continue like this-suspended between hypervigilance and despair, unable to sleep, unable to write, unable to imagine a future where he was anything other than waiting for the next person to die.
